definition: One who makes an appointment, or tryst; one who meets withanother.
An umbelliferous biennial plant (Daucus Carota), of manyvarieties.

A shrub or small tree of the genus Corylus, as the C. avellana,bearing a nut containing a kernel of a mild, farinaceous taste; thefilbert. The American species are C. Americana, which produces thecommon hazelnut, and C. rostrata. See Filbert. Gray.
An artificial or affected manner; show of pride or vanity;haughtiness; as, it is said of a person, he puts on airs. Thackeray.

A black, or brownish black, solid, combustible substance, dugfrom beds or veins in the earth to be used for fuel, and consisting,like charcoal, mainly of carbon, but more compact, and oftenaffording, when heated, a large amount of volatile matter.
Having a general resemblance to lilies or to liliaceous plants.

That quality or condition of a body in virtue of which itexhibits opposite, or contrasted, properties or powers, in opposite,or contrasted, parts or directions; or a condition giving rise to acontrast of properties corresponding to a contrast of positions, as,for example, attraction and repulsion in the opposite parts of amagnet, the dissimilar phenomena corresponding to the different sidesof a polarized ray of light, etc.
See Plaice. [Obs.]
Swimming on the surface; buoyant; light. Sir W. Raleigh.
Pertaining to, or designating, either one of two distinct acidswhich are derived from xylic acid and related compounds, and aremetameric with uvitic acid.
Built with groins; as, a groined ceiling; a groined vault.
Pertaining to a gyrus, or convolution.
Same as 1st Timber. [Scot.]
A defensive garment formerly in use for the body, made of clothstuffed and quilted.
A sheriff's deputy, appointed to make arrests, collect fines,summon juries, etc.

Of or pertaining to Michael Faraday, the distinguishedelectrician; -- applied especially to induced currents ofelectricity, as produced by certain forms of inductive apparatus, onaccount of Faraday's investigations of their laws.
The channel of a river. Weate.

A yellow coal-tar dyestuff which probably consists chiefly ofrosolic acid. See Aurin, and Rosolic acid under Rosolic. Redcorallin, a red dyestuff which is obtained by treating aurin orrosolic acid with ammonia; -- called also pæonin.-- Yellow corallin. See Aurin.
One who, or that which, secures.
The art or act of varnishing in the Japanese manner.
A pledge; a pawn. [Obs.] Gower. Piers Plowman.Let him be ware, his neck lieth to wed [i. e., for a security].Chaucer.
Same as Pterylosis.

Something proposed to be solved by guessing or conjecture; apuzzling question; an ambiguous proposition; an enigma; hence,anything ambiguous or puzzling.To wring from me, and tell to them, my secret, That solved the riddlewhich I had proposed. Milton.'T was a strange riddle of a lady. Hudibras.
A match for lighting candles, lamps, etc.
A tower. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Pertaining to, or derived from, vanilla or vanillin; resemblingvanillin; specifically, designating an alcohol and an acidrespectively, vanillin being the intermediate aldehyde.

The sphere or globular mass of cells (blastomeres), formed bythe clevage of the ovum or egg in the first stages of itsdevelopment; -- called also mulberry mass, segmentation sphere, andblastosphere. See Segmentation.
In a vagrant manner.
A tribute by the head; a capitation tax. [Written also chevageand chivage.] [Obs.]
Morphine.
One who lives by sharking.
Enactment; resolution. [Obs.] Shak.
The eelpout; guffer eel.
A false spur or gaff, fitted on the heel of a gamecock. Wright.
Made of elder. [Obs.]He would discharge us as boys do eldern guns. Marston.
Characterized by, or pertaining to, petechiæ; spotted.Petechial fever, a malignant fever, accompanied with livid spots onthe skin.
That part of the stamen containing the pollen, or fertilizingdust, which, when mature, is emitted for the impregnation of theovary.-- An"ther*al, a.
Of or pertaining to the amnion; characterized by an amnion; as,the amniotic fluid; the amniotic sac. Amniotic acid. (Chem.) [R.] SeeAllantoin.
A genus of crustaceans, containing the crawfish of fresh-waterlobster of Europe, and allied species of western North America. SeeCrawfish.

from Hide. Concealed; put out of view; secret; not known;mysterious. Hidden fifths or octaves (Mus.), consecutive fifths oroctaves, not sounded, but suggested or implied in the parallel motionof two parts towards a fifth or an octave.
See Shawm. [Obs.] Knolles.
Press. [Obs.] Spenser.
To transmit by way of tradition; to hand down. [Obs.]The following story is . . . traditioned with very much creditamongst our English Catholics. Fuller.
An alkaloid obtained from the yellow jasmine (Gelsemiumsempervirens), as a bitter white semicrystalline substance; -- calledalso gelsemia.
One who reships.
The system of bards; the learning and maxims of bards.

A luminous impression produced through excitation of the retinaby some cause other than the impingement upon it of rays of light, asby pressure upon the eyeball when the lids are closed. Cf. After-image.
A soft ointment prepared from oil. Dunglison.
A director. [Obs. & R.] Dr. R. Clerke.
To imitate the manner of the Laconians, especially in brief,pithy speech, or in frugality and austerity.
See Presbyopia.
One who, or that which, incites.
The state or quality of being immane; barbarity. [R.] Shak.
Having the form of a cyme.
To be too trustful or confident; to trust too much. [Obs.]Wyclif
Full of, or consisting of, motes. [Written also mottie.][Scot.]The motty dust reek raised by the workmen. H. Miller.
A rhetorician. [Obs.] Hammond.
Having a nap or pile; downy; shaggy. Holland.
A cuban trogon (Priotelus temnurus) having a serrated bill anda tail concave at the end.
To make unholy; to profane. Tennyson.Nor can the unholiness of the priest dishallow the altar. T. Adams.
A drain trench, in a ditch or moat; -- called also cuvette.
The art of governing a state; statecraft; policy. [Obs.]The enemies of God . . . call our religion statism. South.
A genus of leguminous plants, containing many species, andincluding the sensitive plants (Mimosa sensitiva, and M. pudica).
Same as Rat-tail.
An impure earthy or coaly bitumen, which emits a highly fetidodor when burning.
A bird of the Thrush family.
Wonderfully; wondrously. [Obs.] Chaucer.
A dry measure in Spain and Spanish America, varying from 1 DeColange.
One who covets.
Impairment. [Obs.] Wyclif.
See Color.
A genus of bivalve mollusks, common on the coasts of Americaand Europe.
To plunder; to waste in riot. [Obs.]
A suffrutescent, D. Fraxinella (the only species), with strongperfume and showy flowers. The volatile oil of the leaves is highlyinflammable.
To grow tired; to become exhausted or impatient; as, to wearyof an undertaking.
A shoe that is worn over another for protection from wet or forextra warmth; esp., an India-rubber shoe; a galoche.
To recall what is done by shouting. [Obs.] Shak.
To close again. Pope.
One who catches turtles or tortoises. "The Jamaica turtlers."Dampier.
A representation of the aspects of the celestial bodies for anymoment o at a given event.A blue case, from which was drawn a scheme of nativity. Sir W. Scott.
In a quaking manner; fearfully. Sir P. Sidney.
Balancing; moving like a balance, as it tends to an equipoiseor level.

A small bottle of horn or other material formerly used forholding ink; an inkstand; a portable case for writing materials."With a writer's inkhorn by his side." Ezek. ix. 2.From his pocket the notary drew his papers and inkhorn. Longfellow.
One who levants, or decamps. [Colloq. Eng.]
A light textile fabric, like a fine bunting.
A tenure by which houses or lands are held of the king or otherlord of a borough or city; at a certain yearly rent, or by servicesrelating to trade or handicraft. Burrill.
One who respects. A respecter of persons, one who regards orjudges with partiality.Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons. Acts x.34.
Divided, or deeply cleft, into four parts; as, a quadrifidperianth; a quadrifid leaf.
To render neat; to clean; to put in order. [R.] Chapman.
To sew up, so nicely that the seam is not perceived; to renter.Marryat.
A Russian and German liqueur, consisting of a sweetened spiritflavored with caraway seeds.
A female archer. Markham.
An agreement between belligerents for the exchange ofprisoners. Wilhelm.
Hautboys, or oboes, played by town musicians; not used in thesingular. [Obs.] Halliwell.
Of an azure color; sky-blue. "The azured harebell." Shak.
Somewhat salt.-- Salt"ish*ly, adv.-- Salt"ish*ness, n.
A plant having a woody, durable stem, but less than a tree; ashrub.
State of being pursy.
Of or pertaining to the crow; crowlike.
To separate, prepare, or obtain, by dialysis or osmose; to passthrough an animal membrane; to subject to dialysis. [Written alsodialyse.]
Of or pertaining to the leeches.
One who incurs a penalty of forfeiture.
Situated under, or on the ventral side of, the tail; as, thesubcaudal, or chevron, bones.
The quality of being amorous; lovingness. [R.] Galt.
One who saws; a sawyer.
The thickness of the layer or body of pigment applied by thepainter to his canvas with especial reference to the juxtaposition ofdifferent colors and tints in forming a harmonious whole. Fairholt.
Become wild. [R.]An old garden plant escaped and wilded. J. Earle.
A carver. [Obs.] Chaucer.

A Chinese toy made by cutting a square of thin wood, or othersuitable material, into seven pieces, as shown in the cut, thesepieces being capable of combination in various ways, so as to form agreat number of different figures. It is now often used in primaryschools as a means of instruction.

Not willing to yield or compIy with what is required or isreasonable; perverse; disobedient; peevish; as, a froward child.A froward man soweth strife. Prov. xvi. 28.A froward retention of custom is as turbulent a thing as innovation.Bacon.
An inflammation of the large intestine, esp. of its mucousmembrane; colonitis.
To refuse. [Obs.] Holinshed.
A leaf-cutting bee of the genus Megachilus. See Leaf cutter,under Leaf.

Work adorned with frets; ornamental openwork or work in relief,esp. when elaborate and minute in its parts. Heuce, any minute playof light andshade, dark and light, or the like.Banqueting on the turf in the fretwork of shade and sunshine.Macaulay.
Free from bushes; bare.O'er the long backs of the bushless downs. Tennyson.
A pen, house, or inclosure, for hogs.
Sacrifices offered to the souls of deceased heroes or friends.
Paste used by weavers to dress their webs. Buchanan.
To habituate to a climate not native; to acclimatize. J. H.Newman.
A slender, leafless portion of a plant by which it becomesattached to a supporting body, after which the tendril usuallycontracts by coiling spirally.
Nonjuring.
Destitute of shoes. Addison.
A prefix, in names of Scotch origin, signifying son.
Derived from castor oil; ricinoleic; as, elaiodic acid. [R.]
Ramal.
To lay waste; to ravage; to desolate.Whole countries . . . were devastated. Macaulay.
Nephew. [Obs.] haucer.
One prone to sound or excite alarms, especially, needlessalarms. Macaulay.

Belonging to, or proceeding from, the original stock; native;hence, not counterfeit, spurious, false, or adulterated; authentic;real; natural; true; pure; as, a genuine text; a genuine production;genuine materials. "True, genuine night." Dryden.

The redemption of man from the bondage of sin and liability toeternal death, and the conferring on him of everlasting happiness.To earn salvation for the sons of men. Milton.Godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation. 2. Cor. vii. 10.
Disordered or unsettled in intellect; deranged. [Scot.] Sir W.Scott.
See Jet. [Obs.]
Covered with, or containing, bark. "The barky fingers of theelm." Shak.
Same as Diapason. [Obs.]A tuneful diapase of pleasures. Spenser.
Of or pertaining to the retina. Retinal purple (Physiol.Chem.), the visual purple.
The female of a hawk or falcon.
Having rotted; putrid; decayed; as, a rotten apple; rottenmeat. Hence:(a) Offensive to the smell; fetid; disgusting.You common cry or curs! whose breath I hate As reek of the rottenfens. Shak.
United closely; confederated; chemically united.
A Persian idiom.
An imperfect enunciation of the letter r, in which it soundslike l.
A prickle.
A short, straight, horizontal mark [-], placed over vowels todenote that they are to be pronounced with a long sound; as, a, indame; e, in seam, etc.
Consisting of a thousand; millennial.
A genus of large arenaceous fossil Foraminifera found in theCretaceous rocks. The species are globular, or nearly so, and are ofall sizes up to that of a tennis ball.
To install again. Milton.
A hypothetical radical found in certain derivatives ofstyrolene and cinnamic acid; -- called also cinnyl, or cinnamyl.
One who deals in wine; a wine seller, or wine merchant.
The coloring principle of turmeric, or curcuma root, extractedas an orange yellow crystalline substance, C14H14O4, with a greenfluorescence.
Any plant of the umbelliferous genus Laserpitium, of severalspecies (as L. glabrum, and L. siler), the root of which yields aresinous substance of a bitter taste. The genus is mostly European.
Hence, to rescue and deliver from the bondage of sin and thepenalties of God's violated law.Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a cursefor us. Gal. iii. 13.
The loosely woven substance which lines the chambers within thegleba in certain Gasteromycetes.
See Cherif.
Serving to assuage pain; soothing.The anodyne draught of oblivion. Burke.
The raspberry. [Obs.] Langham.
An assessment or tax. [Obs.] Johnson.
The Chinese name for a highly prized variety of pale greenjade. See Jade.
An incubator for sickly infants, esp. those prematurely born.
Pertaining to, or consisting of, images, pictures, orrepresentations of any kind.
Resembling cartilage.
In a sound manner.
A wind instrument, blown by a single reed, of richer and fullertone than the oboe, which has a double reed. It is the leadinginstrument in a military band.
Originally, cambric or lawn of fine linen; now applied also tocloth of similar texture made of cotton.
In a magical manner; by magic, or as if by magic.
To form into a hydrate; to combine with water.
Of or pertaining to the Monoecia; monoecious.-- n.

The sudden removal of lands or soil from the estate of one manto that of another by an inundation or a current, or by a suddenchange in the course of a river by which a part of the estate of oneman is cut off and joined to the estate of another. The property inthe part thus separated, or cut off, continues in the original owner.Wharton. Burrill.

Any one of numerous species of small South American monkeys ofthe genera Hapale and Midas, family Hapalidæ. They have long softfur, and a hairy, nonprehensile tail. They are often kept as pets.Called also squirrel monkey.
To strike, as with or against anything large or solid; tothump; as, to bump the head against a wall.

Faithfulness; adherence to right; careful and exact observanceof duty, or discharge of obligations. Especially:(a) Adherence to a person or party to which one is bound; loyalty.Whose courageous fidelity was proof to all danger. Macaulay.The best security for the fidelity of men is to make interestcoincide with duty. A. Hamilton.
Of or performance to Argos, the capital of Argolis in Greece.-- n.
An abscess; a swelling filled with purulent matter. [Writtencorruptly imposthume.]

A landowner; also, a collector of land revenue; now, usually, akind of feudatory recognized as an actual proprietor so long as hepays to the government a certain fixed revenue. [Written alsozemindar.] [India]
Writing; document; scroll. [Obs.] "Of every scrit and bond."Chaucer.
To chagrin. [Obs.]
Unconstrained; easy; free. Vanbrugh.
The art of treating diseases of the hands and feet.
The character or qualities of a saint.
A genus of flowerless plants, having articulated stems andwhorled branches. They flourish in wet places.
To endow. [Obs.] Waterhouse.
To heat to excess; to superheat. Cowper.
The yellow fever in its worst form, when it is usually attendedwith black vomit. See Black vomit.

A winged horse fabled to have sprung from the body of Medusawhen she was slain. He is noted for causing, with a blow of his hoof,Hippocrene, the inspiring fountain of the Muses, to spring from MountHelicon. On this account he is, in modern times, associated with theMuses, and with ideas of poetic inspiration.Each spurs his jaded Pegasus apace. Byron.
One who, or that which, iodizes.
One who smites.I give my back to the smiters. Isa. l. 6.
To make hollow or become hollow like a fistula, or pipe. [Obs.]"A fistulated ulcer." Fuller.
Supplied or covered with wood, or trees; as, land wooded andwatered.The brook escaped from the eye down a deep and wooded dell. Sir W.Scott.

A white robe with a purple border, worn by a Roman boy beforehe was entitled to wear the toga virilis, or until about thecompletion of his fourteenth year, and by girls until their marriage.It was also worn by magistrates and priests.
A written or printed notice to be posted, as on a wall; aposter; a placard.
In a general sense, denoting from or away from; as:
To surpass in sounding.
A tribe of North American Indians formerly inhabiting thecountry from the upper Missouri River to the Saskatchewan, but nowmuch reduced in numbers.
Tenth. [Obs.]Every tithe soul, 'mongst many thousand. Shak.
Evidence; declaration. [Obs.]The sensible and true avouch Of mine own eyes. Shak.
To give a nickname to. Camden.
The chaparral cock.
A genus of spiral gastropod shells, often of large size,characteristic of the lower Silurian rocks.
A small armed vessel, with sails and oars, -- used on theMalabar coast. A. Chalmers.
Containing an ovule or ovules.
Made.  Chaucer.
The roebuck.
A salt of prussic acid; a cyanide. Red prussiate of potash. SeePotassium ferricyanide, under Ferricyanide. Yellow prussiate ofpotash. See Potassium ferrocyanide, under Ferrocyanide.
Made or done after the date assigned.Of these [predictions] some were postdate; cunningly made after thething came to pass. Fuller.
One who kills a fox, except in hunting; also, the act of sokilling a fox. [Written also vulpecide.]
See Ascus.
Quiet; calm; undisturbed; peaceful; not agitated; as, theatmosphere is tranquil; the condition of the country is tranquil.A style clear, tranquil, easy to follow. De Quincey.
In a secular or worldly manner.
Long-horned; pertaining to the Longicornia.-- n.
One who conquers. The Conqueror (Eng. Hist.). William theNorman (1027-1067) who invaded England, defeated Harold in the battleof Hastings, and was crowned king, in 1066.
Animating; cheering; moving; exhilarating; as, an inspiring orscene.
With attachment; with interest; earnestly.
One of the three jurisdictions into which the county of York,in England, is divided; -- formerly under the government of reeve.They are called the North, the East, and the West, Riding.Blackstone.
A shrew. [Obs.] Shak.
See Pontee.
In the organ, a light strip of wood connecting (in path) a keyand a pallet, to communicate motion by pulling.

The berry of the pimento (Eugenia pimenta), a tree of the WestIndies; a spice of a mildly pungent taste, and agreeably aromatic;Jamaica pepper; pimento. It has been supposed to combine the flavorof cinnamon, nutmegs, and cloves; and hence the name. The name isalso given to other aromatic shrubs; as, the Carolina allspice(Calycanthus floridus); wild allspice (Lindera benzoin), called alsospicebush, spicewood, and feverbush.
Banishment. [R.] Sir. H. Wotton.
A tree or shrub bearing cones; one of the order Coniferae,which includes the pine, cypress, and (according to some) the yew.
See 1st Fluke.
An additional or extra tax.
A yellow crystalline substance resembling quinone, extractedfrom green shucks of the walnut (Juglans regia); -- called alsonucin.
A plane figure having four sides and angles; a quadrangle, as asquare, a rhombus, etc.
The whole axial portion of an animal, including the head, neck,trunk, and tail. B. G. Wilder.
The sodium salt of a sulphonic acid of a naphthol,C10H5(OH)(NH2)SO3Na used as a developer.
The act of detorting, or the state of being detorted; atwisting or warping.
Same as 4th Lunge.
Rimose.
One who assigns, appoints, allots, or apportions.
A debt; an entry on the debtor (Dr.) side of an account; --mostly used adjectively; as, the debit side of an account.
To cover up. Shak.
Leprosy.
To convert into vapor, as by the application of heat, whethernaturally or artificially. Vaporizing surface. (Steam Boilers) SeeEvaporating surface, under Evaporate, v. t.

A bright silver-white metallic element. It is of the irongroup, and is hard, malleable, and ductile. It occurs combined withsulphur in millerite, with arsenic in the mineral niccolite, and witharsenic and sulphur in nickel glance. Symbol Ni. Atomic weight 58.6.
A despising; contempt. [R.]A despisal of religion. South.
A large Mediterranean food fish (Umbrina cirrhosa): -- calledalso umbra, and umbrine.
The state of being a pauper; the state of indigent personsrequiring support from the community. Whatly.
A kind of frock for children.
A river in the Nether World or infernal regions; also, theinfernal regions themselves. By some of the English poets it wassupposed to be a flaming lake or gulf. Shak.
Capable of being classed.
Pertaining to, or situated near, the anus; as, the anal fin orglands.
To lay (a figure) upon another in such a manner that all theparts of the one coincide with the parts of the other; as, tosuperpose one plane figure on another.
The quality of state or being brave.
One of two species of large South African antelopes of thegenus Catoblephas, having a mane and bushy tail, and curved horns inboth sexes. [Written also gnoo.]
In an unwary manner.
An arrow, having a rotary motion, formerly used with thecrossbow. Cf. Vireton. Gower.
One who serves on board of the same ship with another; a fellowsailor.

An implacable or malicious foe; one who is diabolically wickedor cruel; an infernal being; -- applied specifically to the devil ora demon.Into this wild abyss the wary fiend Stood on the brink of Hell andlooked a while. Milton.O woman! woman! when to ill thy mind Is bent, all hell contains nofouler fiend. Pope.
Parsley. [Obs.] Chaucer.
The papacy. [Obs.] Milton.
A substance from the yolk of salmon's egg.
To lie over or upon; specifically, to suffocate by lying upon;as, to overlie an infant. Quain.A woman by negligence overlieth her child in her sleeping. Chaucer.
Conveyance by boat; also, a charge for such conveyance.
A platform; the bottom of a room; a floor; pavement. See Floor,n. Addison.
To cease from being ruffled or agitated. Dryden.
See Maslin.
The first vertebra of the neck, articulating immediately withthe skull, thus sustaining the globe of the head, whence the name.
Giving assent; of the nature of assent; complying.-- As*sent"ive*ness, n.

The formal decision, or expression of views, of a judge, anumpire, a counselor, or other party officially called upon toconsider and decide upon a matter or point submitted. To be ofopinion, to think; to judge.-- To hold opinion with, to agree with. [Obs.] Shak.

A member of that party, among the Scotch seceders, whichasserted the lawfulness of the burgess oath (in which burgessesprofess "the true religion professed within the realm"), the oppositeparty being called antiburghers.
To move heavily; to lounge or idle; to loll. [Law.] CharlesReade.
Of or pertaining to the main or great sea; as, the ocean waves;an ocean stream. Milton.
The crested titmouse. [Prov. Eng.]
Any aquatic mammal of the order Cetacea, especially any one ofthe large species, some of which become nearly one hundred feet long.Whales are hunted chiefly for their oil and baleen, or whalebone.
A white opacity in the cornea of the eye; -- called alsoalbugo.
In a willing manner; with free will; without reluctance;cheerfully. Chaucer.The condition of that people is not so much to be envied as somewould willingly represent it. Addison.

To lead into danger by artifice; to lure into a net or snare;to entrap; to insnare; to allure; to entice; as, to decoy troops intoan ambush; to decoy ducks into a net.Did to a lonely cot his steps decoy. Thomson.E'en while fashion's brightest arts decoy, The heart, distrusting,asks if this be joy. Goldsmith.
Broken, as an ordinary; cut off, or broken at the top, as achevron, a bend, or the like.
To deprive of glasslike character; to take away vitreous lusterand transparency from.
The state or quality of being a lady; the personality of alady.
A cuirass. [Obs.] Spenser.
Of or derived from angelica; as, angelic acid; angelic ether.Angelic acid, an acid obtained from angelica and some other plants.
One of a class of fabled female water spirits who might receivea human soul by intermarrying with a mortal.
One who passes; a passenger.
To weed, or clear of weeds, with a hoe. [Obs.] Ainsworth.
Having the property of dichroism; as, a dichroic crystal.
The part of a tree which lies immediately under the bark; thealburnum or sapwood.

A South African shrub (Barosma) with small leaves that aredotted with oil dlands; also, the leaves themselves, which are usedin medicine for diseases of the urinary organs, etc. Several speciesfurnish the leaves.
A layer of tiles forming a corona for a wall.
Resembling, or allied to, the genus Oreodon.
A movable part of a rail; or of opposite rails, fortransferring cars from one track to another.
The menstrual flux; menses. [Obs.]
State of being fluxible.[Obs.]
Coming into being; nascent. [Obs.] Bp. Warburton.
A shrike or butcher bird; -- called also mattages. [Prov. Eng.]
One who desponds.

Capable of neutralizing, or of combining with, severalmolecules of a monobasic acid; having more than one hydrogen atomcapable of being replaced by acid radicals; -- said of certain bases;as, calcium hydrate and glycerin are polyacid bases.

A wild or uncultivated plant; especially, a wild apple tree orcrab apple; also, the fruit of such a plant. Spenser.Ten ruddy wildings in the wood I found. Dryden.The fruit of the tree . . . is small, of little juice, and badquality. I presume it to be a wilding. Landor.
Without pause or end; incessant.
A polypidom.
Æolian, 1; as, the Æolic dialect; the Æolic mode.

An element of the chromium group, found in certain rareminerals, as pitchblende, uranite, etc., and reduced as a heavy,hard, nickel-white metal which is quite permanent. Its yellow oxideis used to impart to glass a delicate greenish-yellow tint which isaccompanied by a strong fluorescence, and its black oxide is used asa pigment in porcelain painting. Symbol U. Atomic weight 239.
One who thinks; especially and chiefly, one who thinks in aparticular manner; as, a close thinker; a deep thinker; a coherentthinker.
See Sermonizer.
A suite; a set of variations.
Environment.

Incapable of being seen; not perceptible by vision; notvisible.To us invisible, or dimly seen In these thy lowest works. Milton.Invisible bird (Zoöl.), a small, shy singing bird (Myadestessibilons), of St. Vincent Islands.-- Invisible green, a very dark shade of green, approaching toblack, and liable to be mistaken for it.
A computer.
The eland. [Written also impoofoo.]
A mass ccomposed of various materials confusedly mixed; amedley; a mixture.A confounded farrago of doubts, fears, hopes, wishes, and all theflimsy furniture of a country miss's brain. Sheridan.
Of or pertaining to the clergy; clerical; clerkily; learned.[Obs.] Milton.
The word which unites the subject and predicate.
A plan proposed; a draft of a proposed measure; a project.
One who invades; an assailant; an encroacher; an intruder.
To thrive poorly; to be not thrifty or prosperous. [Obs.]

The organ formed by the combination or union into one body ofstem and leaf, and often bearing the fructification; as, the frond ofa fern or of a lichen or seaweed; also, the peculiar leaf of a palmtree.
Serving to aid or help; serving as a chapel of ease; tributary.[R.]Not a city was without its cathedral, surrounded by its succursalchurches, its monasteries, and convents. Milman.
A false wall; a work raised in front of the main wall. [Writtenalso vaimure, and vamure.] Camden.
With a hissing sound.
Of or pertaining to statistics; as, statistical knowledge,statistical tabulation.
A small shaft sunk from one level to another, as for thepurpose of ventilation.
That which is obvious, public, or common.Dealing out exoteries only to the vulgar. A. Tucker.
One who, or that which, glides.
See Morrow. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Carrion; any filth. [Prob. Eng.] Halliwell.
Like, or having the qualities of, antimony; antimonial.
One who forges, makes, of forms; a fabricator; a falsifier.
Pertaining to Romanism.
Suiting a funeral; pertaining to burial; solemn. Hence: Dark;dismal; mournful. Jer. Taylor.What seem to us but sad funereal tapers May be heaven's distantlamps. Longfellow.-- Fu*ne"re*al*ly, adv.
One who uses a scythe; a mower. Macaulay.
Var. of Karakul, a kind of fur.
A channel or furrow.
A halfpenny. [Spelt also baubee.] [Scot. & Prov. Eng.]
A spasmodic trembling of the upper eyelid.
A cod salted and dried. Ainsworth.

Having the characteristics of Circe, daughter of Sol andPerseis, a mythological enchantress, who first charmed her victimsand then changed them to the forms of beasts; pleasing, but noxious;as, a Circean draught.
A sharp-pointed tool, used by joiners for drawing lines onstuff; a marking awl.
Quality of being spiny.
The unit of electric induction; the induction in a circuit whenthe electro-motive force induced in this circuit is one volt, whilethe inducing current varies at the rate of one ampère a second.
To examine or investigate judicially; to examine by witnessesor other judicial evidence and the principles of law; as, to try acause, or a criminal.
Of or pertaining to monks or a monastic life; monastic.
In a disorderly manner. [Obs.] Rom. of R.
A tract of soft, wet ground; a marsh; a fen. Morass ore. (Min.)See Bog ore, under Bog.
See Edentate, a.-- n. (Zoöl.)
The lees of beer, cider, etc.; yeast. [U.S.]
See Waivure. [R.]
To work sluggishly or slowly; to plod. [Obs.]
A mowing, or that which is gathered by mowing; -- chiefly usedin composition; as, an aftermath. [Obs.]The first mowing thereof, for the king's use, is wont to be soonerthan the common math. Bp. Hall.
To cause to resemble a dandy; to make dandyish.
A viola da gamba.
To confirm; to render valid; to give legal force to.The chamber of deputies . . . refusing to validate at once theelection of an official candidate. London Spectator.
To make wintry. [Obs.]
Murrhine.
Odd in manner or appearance; fantastic; whimsical; extravagant;grotesque. C. Kingsley.

A word of doubtful meaning, occuring frequently in the Psalms;by some, supposed to signify silence or a pause in the musicalperformance of the song.Beyond the fact that Selach is a musical term, we know absolutelynothing about it. Dr. W. Smith (Bib. Dict.)
See Afrit.
Pertaining to, or derived from, oxalic acid and aniline; --used to designate an acid obtained in white crystalline scales byheating these substances together.
Free from pain; without pain.-- Pain"less*ly, adv.-- Pain"less*ness, n.
Growing under ground; remaining under ground; ripening itsfruit under ground. [Written also hypogæous.]
A fragrant flower. Tennyson.
A celebrated Greek epic poem, in twenty-four books, on thedestruction of Ilium, the ancient Troy. The Iliad is ascribed toHomer.
To bully. [Obs.]She shan't think to bullock and domineer over me. Foote.
Harbor dues; port dues.
Toothed; with teeth. [R] Croxall.

Absorbing; swallowing; absorptive. Absorbent ground (Paint.), aground prepared for a picture, chiefly with distemper, or watercolors, by which the oil is absorbed, and a brilliancy is imparted tothe colors.

A brown or reddish pigment used in both oil and water colors,obtained from certain natural clays variously colored by the oxidesof iron and manganese. It is commonly heated or burned before beingused, and is then called burnt umber; when not heated, it is calledraw umber. See Burnt umber, below.
A contrivance for adjusting or regulating the strength ofelectrical currents, operating usually by the intercalation ofresistance which can be varied at will. Wheatstone. --Rhe`o*stat"ic,a.
Resembling a little stake.
The production and excretion of bile.
A Mass for a deceased person or for some special object, saiddaily for a year or on the anniversary day.
A small or young stem.
To emasculate; to dispossess of manhood. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.
The little stalk that attaches a seed to the placenta.
Same as Fugleman.
To avail. [Obs.]
The state of an heir; succession by inheritance. Burke.
One of a tribe of beetles, having long maxillary palpi.
An alkaloid found with hyoscyamine (with which it is alsoisomeric) in henbane, and extracted as a white, amorphous, semisolidsubstance.
A band of minute tubercles, bearing modified spines, on theshells of spatangoid sea urchins. See Spatangoidea.
An oily liquid, resembling, and possibly identical with,furfurol, and obtained from fucus, and other seaweeds.
The quality or state of being new; as, the newness of a system;the newness of a scene; newness of life.

To talk or confer secretly and confidentially; to converse,especially with evil intentions; to plot mischief. [Archaic orColloq.]Pray go in; and, sister, salve the matter, Collogue with her again,and all shall be well. Greene.He had been colloguing with my wife. Thackeray.
The impression of the foot; a trace or footmark; as,"Footprints of the Creator."

That is to be or come hereafter; that will exist at any timeafter the present; as, the next moment is future, to the present.Future tense (Gram.), the tense or modification of a verb whichexpresses a future act or event.
Ruttish; lustful.

To wash or strain out so as to purify; as, to elutriate theblood as it passes through the lungs; to strain off or decant, as apowder which is separated from heavier particles by being drawn offwith water; to cleanse, as by washing.
Same as Serolin (b).

To make a solemn declaration under oath or affirmation, for thepurpose of establishing, or making proof of, some fact to a court; togive testimony in a cause depending before a tribunal.One witness shall not testify against any person to cause him to die.Num. xxxv. 30.

A second or reciprocal distress of other goods in lieu of goodswhich were taken by a first distress and have been eloigned; a takingby way of reprisal; -- chiefly used in the expression capias inwithernam, which is the name of a writ used in connection with theaction of replevin (sometimes called a writ of reprisal), whichissues to a defendant in replevin when he has obtained judgment for areturn of the chattels replevied, and fails to obtain them on thewrit of return. Blackstone.
A female or hen eagle. [R.] Sherwood.
The stone at the foot of a grave; -- opposed to headstone.
Only; merely; singly. [Obs.]This said spirit was not given alonely unto him, but unto all hisheirs and posterity. Latimer.

A large tree of genus Melia (M. Azadirachta) found in India.Its bark is bitter, and used as a tonic. A valuable oil is expressedfrom its seeds, and a tenacious gum exudes from its trunk. The M.Azedarach is a much more showy tree, and is cultivated in theSouthern United States, where it is known as Pride of India, Pride ofChina, or bead tree. Various parts of the tree are consideredanthelmintic.The margosa oil . . . is a most valuable balsam for wounds, having apeculiar smell which prevents the attacks of flies. Sir S. Baker.
A dolt; a blockhead. [Obs.] Bp. Parker.
Having the edge worn away so as to be jagged or irregularlytoothed.
A peculiar kind of reproductive cell found in certain fungi,and often containing zoöspores.
Gentle; courteous; complaisant; yielding. [Obs.]
Pertaining to a poem, or to poetry; poetical. [R.] Coleridge.
To develop again; specif. (Photog.),
Inhabiting the seashore, esp. the zone between high-water andlow-water mark.
Characterized by a current which flows inward; as, theincurrent orifice of lamellibranch Mollusca.
Having life; -- used only in composition; as, long-lived;short-lived.
An ancient war engine for hurling stones.
A plasterer's float, having two handles; -- used in smoothingceilings, etc.
A genus of birds comprising the wrynecks.
The European widgeon. [Prov. Eng.]
To stone. [Obs.]
Ounce by ounce.
A condition in which there are two beats or waves of thearterial pulse to each beat of the heart.
To blow through. [Obs.] Harvey.
Natural advantaged; endowments; accomplishments. [R.] "Thebenefits of your own country." Shak. Benefit of clergy. (Law) Seeunder Clergy.
Dizzy; giddy. [Prov. Eng.]
A small nematoid worm (Oxyurus vermicularis), which isparasitic chiefly in the rectum of man. It is most common in childrenand aged persons.
A form of crystal common with quartz, consisting of two six-sided pyramids, base to base.
To stun. [Obs.] "Breathless and astunned." Somerville.
In the form of pus.
Great heat, as of the body in fever.
A Ceylonese boat. See Doni.

An order of wingless hexapod insects which have setiform caudalappendages, either bent beneath the body to form a spring, orprojecting as bristles. It comprises the Cinura, or bristletails, andthe Collembola, or springtails. Called also Thysanoura. See Lepisma,and Podura.
A pool or lake. Drayton. Tennyson.
A conglomerate or grit rock, consisting of rounded pebbles sandfirmly united together.
Any one of family (Uroceridæ) of large hyminopterous insects,allied to the sawflies. The larvæ bore in the wood of trees. Socalled from the long, stout ovipositors of the females.
Pertaining to moss of the genus Sphagnum, or bog moss;abounding in peat or bog moss.

Accompanying as a subordinate; aiding in a secondary way;additional; connected as an incident or subordinate to a principal;contributing or contributory; said of persons and things, and, whenof persons, usually in a bad sense; as, he was accessory to the riot;accessory sounds in music.
Six.
Furnished with a parson.
The ruins of the fallen roof resulting from the removal of thepillars and stalls. Raymond.
The party to a contract who receives, or agrees to receive, theproperty sold. Blackstone.
Done or recurring every ninth year.
The office of a priest. [Obs.] Milton.
Of or pertaining to the mineral jargon.
Any sight or reading of the leveling staff, except thebacksight; any sight or bearing taken by a compass or theodolite in aforward direction.
To thrust away. [Obs.] Johnson.
The breast beam of a loom.
A private friend; a confidential friend; a confidant. [Obs.]Fuller.
A small spark. [Obs.]
A duel; the decision of a case by a duel.
Not amiable; morose; ill-natured; repulsive.-- Un*a"mi*a*bly, adv.
The end of the vertebral column beyond the sacrum in man andtailless monkeys. It is composed of several vertebræ more or lessconsolidated.
Black and blue; grayish blue; of a lead color; discolored, asflesh by contusion. Cowper.There followed no carbuncles, no purple or livid spots, the mass ofthe blood not being tainted. Bacon.
OF or pertaining to rotary motion; having power to draw out orturn round. "By art trochilic." Camden.
A fish resembling the trout. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Garew.
A genus of small, bivalve, freshwater Crustacea, belonging tothe Ostracoda; also, a member of this genus.
To elect or choose beforehand. [R.] Walter Harte.
To amalgamate and blend; to beat up or mix in water, as clay.
Duskiness. [R.] Sir T. Elyot.
A grandfather. [Obs.] Writ of Ayle, an ancient English writwhich lay against a stranger who had dispossessed the demandant ofland of which his grandfather died seized.
The brow or hairy arch above the eye. Shak.

Pursuits; duties; affairs which occupy one's time; usualemployment; vocation.There are professions, among the men, no more favorable to thesestudies than the common avocations of women. Richardson.In a few hours, above thirty thousand men left his standard, andreturned to their ordinary avocations. Macaulay.An irregularity and instability of purpose, which makes them choosethe wandering avocations of a shepherd, rather than the more fixedpursuits of agriculture. Buckle.
A printed and stitched book containing only a few leaves; apamphlet.
Ornamental work with rambled lines. Especially: --(a) The decorative head of a Gothic window.
To portray; to draw. [Obs.] Spenser.
In a roving, idle manner.
A burst of sunlight.
The science of causes. Same as tiology.
Pertaining to, or consisting of, a sheaf or sheaves; resemblinga sheaf.

To put on the other tack by dropping the lee anchor as soon asthe wind is out of the sails (which brings the vessel's head to thewind), and by cutting the cable as soon as she pays off on the othertack. Clubhauling is attempted only in an exigency.
An auxiliary part of a machine which supplies or leads alongthe material operated upon.
Absent-minded; lost in thought; abstracted.
One to whom a fine of land was ackowledged. Blackstone.
The gadfly of cattle.
To shoot upward. "Trees upshooting high." Spenser.

A North American aquatic fur-bearing rodent (Fiber zibethicus).It resembles a rat in color and having a long scaly tail, but thetail is compressed, the bind feet are webbed, and the ears areconcealed in the fur. It has scent glands which secrete a substancehaving a strong odor of musk. Called also musquash, musk beaver, andondatra.
Ornamented with crockets.
A glucoside found in the stems of the jalap plant and scammony.It is a strong purgative.
Of or pertaining to a canton or cantons; of the nature of acanton.
Same as Thrasher.
To divest of the quality of wonder or mystery; to interpret; toexplain. [R.] Fuller.
A bench on which work is performed, as in a carpenter's shop.
Lying at, or extending toward, the side; away from the mesialplane; external; -- opposed to mesial.
The Syrian bear. See under Bear. [Written also dhubb, and dub.]
One who monishes; an admonisher. [Archaic]
Having numerous or conspicuous veins; veiny; as, a venosefrond.
A fine sieve; a searce. [Obs.]

To rust with violence; to move impetuously; to strikeviolently; as, the waves dash upon rocks.[He] dashed through thick and thin. Dryden.On each hand the gushing waters play, And down the rough cascade alldashing fall. Thomson.
An exemplar; also, a copy of a book or writing. [Obs.] Donne.
Any single emblem or charge in an escutcheon or coat of arms --commonly in the pl.A carriage covered with armorial bearings. Thackeray.
That part of anatomy which treats of muscles.
A boast. See Crack, n. [Obs.] Spenser.
Having colors like those of the rainbow; iridescent. Holmes.
A salt of rutic acid.
See Seep. [Scot. & U.S.]
Having no distinction of sex; sexless; neuter.
See Mastic.
Eggs beaten up with a little flour, etc., and cooked in afrying pan; as, a plain omelet.
See Greggoe.
The bleating of a sheep. Marryat.

Doing the same thing over again; accomplishing a given resultmany times in succession; as, a repeating firearm; a repeating watch.Repeating circle. See the Note under Circle, n., 3.-- Repeating decimal (Arith.), a circulating decimal. See underDecimal.-- Repeating firearm, a firearm that may be discharged many times inquick succession; especially: (a) A form of firearm so constructedthat by the action of the mechanism the charges are successivelyintroduced from a chamber containing them into the breech of thebarrel, and fired. (b) A form in which the charges are held in, anddischarged from, a revolving chamber at the breech of the barrel. SeeRevolver, and Magazine gun, under Magazine.-- Repeating instruments (Astron. & Surv.), instruments forobserving angles, as a circle, theodolite, etc., so constructed thatthe angle may be measured several times in succession, and different,but successive and contiguous, portions of the graduated limb, beforereading off the aggregate result, which aggregate, divided by thenumber of measurements, gives the angle, freed in a measure fromerrors of eccentricity and graduation.-- Repeating watch. See Repeater (a)
A giving suck; the secretion and yielding of milk by themammary gland.
A pupil; a student.
See Dais. [Scot.]
A beef; a beef creature.They would knock down the first beeve they met with. W. Irving.
See under Zygosphene.
A very small chevrotain (Tragulus Javanicus), native of Java.It is about the size of a hare, and is noted for its agility inleaping. Called also Java musk deer, pygmy musk deer, and deerlet.
Somewhat like resin.
See Smolder.

Any large macrurous crustacean used as food, esp. those of thegenus Homarus; as the American lobster (H. Americanus), and theEuropean lobster (H. vulgaris). The Norwegian lobster (NephropsNorvegicus) is similar in form. All these have a pair of largeunequal claws. The spiny lobsters of more southern waters, belongingto Palinurus, Panulirus, and allied genera, have no large claws. Thefresh-water crayfishes are sometimes called lobsters. Lobstercaterpillar (Zoöl.), the caterpillar of a European bombycid moth(Stauropus fagi); -- so called from its form. Lobster louse (Zoöl.),a copepod crustacean (Nicothoë astaci) parasitic on the gills of theEuropean lobster.
Same as Bear's-foot.
A shield or target. [Obs. or Poetic] "A buckler on a targe."Chaucer.

The number nine or a group of nine. The Enneads, the titlegiven to the works of the philosopher Plotinus, published by hispupil Porphyry; -- so called because each of the six books into whichit is divided contains nine chapters.
See Zinc. [Obs.]
Any one of several species of beautiful birds of Australia andNew Guinea, of the genera Ptiloris and Craspidophora, allied to theparadise birds.
A common European wild pigeon (Columba ænas), so called becauseat one time believed to be the stock of the domestic pigeon, or,according to some, from its breeding in the stocks, or trunks, oftrees.
That part of the large intestines which extends from the cæcumto the rectum.

Capable of being permeated, or passed through; yieldingpassage; passable; penetrable; -- used especially of substances whichallow the passage of fluids; as, wood is permeable to oil; glass ispermeable to light. I. Taylor.

In Japanese costume and decorative art, a small object carvedin wood, ivory, bone, or horn, or wrought in metal, and pierced withholes for cords by which it is connected, for convenience, with theinro, the smoking pouch (tabako-ire), and similar objects carried inthe girdle. It is now much used on purses sold in Europe and America.
An elephant having large tusks.
A sack or bag of wool; specifically, the seat of the lordchancellor of England in the House of Lords, being a large, squaresack of wool resembling a divan in form.
Lost or alienated for an offense or crime; liable to penalseizure.Thy wealth being forfeit to the state. Shak.To tread the forfeit paradise. Emerson.
A thin, pointed nail, with a heavy flaring head, for securing ahorsehoe to the hoof; a horsehoe nail.
An Arabian shrub Catha edulis) the leaves of which are used astea by the Arabs.

A genus of small beetles, several of which, in the larvalstate, are very destructive to woolen goods, fur, etc. The common"museum pest" is A. varius; the carpet beetle is A. scrophulariæ. Thelarvæ are commonly confounded with moths.
A hill; a cliff. [Obs.] Spenser.

A large, extinct bird (Didus ineptus), formerly inhabiting theIsland of Mauritius. It had short, half-fledged wings, like those ofthe ostrich, and a short neck and legs; -- called also dronte. It wasrelated to the pigeons.
Change; alteration, either in form or qualities.The vicissitude or mutations in the superior globe are no fit matterfor this present argument. Bacon.
To make mysterious; to make a mystery of.
A small thicket or grove with undergrowth; a clump of trees.[Written also spinney, and spinny.]The downs rise steep, crowned with black fir spinnies. C. Kingsley.
See Pucelle. [Obs.]
Too weak; too feeble.
The belief or doctrine that attributes everything to nature asa sanative agent.
Same as Hypostasis, 2.
A writer or drawer up of papal bulls. [R.] Harmar.
One who piks or chooses; esp., an inspector who select waressuitable for market.
To mix; to mingle. [R.]Amongst her tears immixing prayers meek. Spenser.
Passing to the west.Toward heaven's descent had sloped his westering wheel. Milton.
Sullenly; threateningly; maliciously; so as to produceblackness.
Of or pertaining to actinism; as, actinic rays.

To chide with vehemence; to scold; to censure violently.Spencer.Go, rate thy minions, proud, insulting boy! Shak.Conscience is a check to beginners in sin, reclaiming them from it,and rating them for it. Barrow.
A poison separable from decomposed meat infusions, and supposedto be formed from albuminous matter through the agency of bacteria.
A friar of a mendicant order (the Order of Our Lady of MountCarmel) established on Mount Carmel, in Syria, in the twelfthcentury; a White Friar.
The first Sunday after Easter; Low Sunday.
See Fane. [Obs.] Joye.
The giving of evidence on the part of a plaintiff to destroythe effect of evidence introduced by the defendant in the same suit.
See Apparel. [Obs.] "In the parail of a pilgrim." PiersPlowman.
The triad, or trinity, of Hindoo gods, consisting of Brahma,the Creator, Vishnu, the Preserver, and Siva, the Destroyer. [Spelledalso Trimurtti.]
Wasteful; rapacious. [Poetic]
The common name of the several species of the genus Parietaria,low, harmless weeds of the Nettle family; -- also called wallpellitory, and lichwort.
To be fastened by a button or buttons; as, the coat will notbutton.
Without shame. L. Addison.
To impress or mark with a seam or cicatrix. Pope.
A double triplet; a group of six equal notes played in the timeof four.
Same as Questor.
The lapwing. [Prov. Eng.]
To break into crumbs or small pieces with the fingers; as, tocrumb bread. [Written also crum.]
Of or pertaining to the second degree.
Settled pay or compensation for services, whether paid daily,monthly, or annually.
The stannel. [Prov. Eng.]
To shelter, as in a haven. Keats.
Situated at the highest part or point. The Supreme, theAlmighty; God.

An optical toy, in which figures made to revolve on the insideof a cylinder, and viewed through slits in its circumference, appearlike a single figure passing through a series of natural motions asif animated or mechanically moved.
A superior kind of dimity made in India, -- used for bedcoverings. [Written also palampore, palampoor, etc.] De Colange.
One who uses irony.
A clerk, precentor, singer, or leader of music, in the church.
A genus of lizards which belong to the family Iguanidæ. Theytake the place in the New World of the chameleons in the Old, and inAmerica are often called chameleons.
To berhyme.
A cavern or cavity, esp. an anatomical cavity or sinus. Huxley.
One who seconds or supports what another attempts, affirms,moves, or proposes; as, the seconder of an enterprise or of a motion.
Careful; wary; cautious; not rash, reckless, or spendthrift;saving; frugal.His rising reputation made him more chary of his fame. Jeffrey.
The more transparent cells, which finally become external, inmany segmenting ova, as those of mammals.
A shrill, somewhat prolonged cry.
A pigeon of the genus Columba and various related genera. Thespecies are numerous.
Pertaining to an acrobat.-- Ac`ro*bat"ic*al*ly, adv.
The body or the head of a comet.
The dorsal portion of an arthromere or somite of an articulateanimal. See Illust. under Coleoptera.
To make a hissing sound; to fry, or to dry and shrivel up, witha hissing sound. [Prov. Eng. & Colloq. U. S.] Forby.
Acritan. Owen.
A black, granular, explosive substance, consisting of anintimate mechanical mixture of niter, charcoal, and sulphur. It isused in gunnery and blasting.
A transparent, colorless oil obtained from elemi resin bydistillation with water; also, a crystallizable extract from theresin.
See Organling.
The act of eloping; secret departure; -- said of a woman and aman, one or both, who run away from their homes for marriage or forcohabitation.
Same as Oillet.
Remitting; forgiving; abating. Bp. Hacket.
A short piece of rope having a knot at one or both ends, with alanyard under the knot, -- used to secure something. Totten.
Of, pertaining to, or resembling, a horse.The shoulders, body, things, and mane are equine; the head completelybovine. Sir J. Barrow.

A certificate of interest due, printed at the bottom oftransferable bonds (state, railroad, etc.), given for a term ofyears, designed to be cut off and presented for payment when theinterest is due; an interest warrant.
A wall-like mass of mineral matter, usually an intrusion ofigneous rocks, filling up rents or fissures in the original strata.
The black tern. [Prov. Eng.]
A hollow in the side of a hill, where game usually lies. "Fleetfoot on the correi." Sir W. Scott.
To swallow up or overwhelm in, or as in, a gulf; to cast into agulf. See Engulf.A river large . . . Passed underneath ingulfed. Milton.
A balance wheel, as of a watch, or clock. See Balance wheel (inthe Vocabulary).
Swelled out like a balloon.
One of the dowels joining the ends of the fellies which formthe circle of the wheel of a gun carriage. Wilhelm.
Like a saint; becoming a holy person.So dear to Heaven is saintly chastity. Milton.

To throw or pull down; to raze; to destroy the fabric of; topull to pieces; to ruin; as, to demolish an edifice, or a wall.I expected the fabric of my book would long since have beendemolished, and laid even with the ground. Tillotson.
One who favors or adheres strictly to a liturgy. Milton.
To move. [Obs.] Thomson.
The cormorant. [Prov. Eng.]
To make great; to enlarge; to magnify. [Obs.] Fotherby.
Lightening. [R.]
To extend under, or be opposed to; as, the line of a trianglewhich subtends the right angle; the chord subtends an arc.
To weigh or press down.A different sin downweighs them to the bottom. Longfellow.
To manifest sullenness; to sulk. [Colloq.]
Easy to be led; governable, as a woman by her husband. [Obs.]Jacob.
In an inhuman manner; cruelly; barbarously.
The crime against nature; sodomy.
Pertaining to, or containing, titanium; as, a titaniticmineral.
A part of a rock or stratum lying without, or beyond, the mainbody, from which it has been separated by denudation.
Zaffer.
Want of faith; distrust. "[Anger] born of your misfaith."Tennyson.
Vitelline.
An Australian honeysucker (Myzomela sanguineolata); -- socalled from the bright red color of the male bird.
imp. & p. p. of Pi, or Pie, v.
Same as Templet.
Out of which. [R.]The cleft whereout the lightning breaketh. Holland.
A voracious, toothed whale of the genus Orca, of which severalspecies are known.
A sexual zooid produced as a medusoid bud upon a hydroid,sometimes becoming a free hydromedusa, sometimes remaining attached.See Hydroidea, and Illusts. of Athecata, Campanularian, and Gonosome.
The doctrine that all things are subject to fate, or that theytake place by inevitable necessity.
According to a square or rule; perpendicular; forming a rightangle. Specifically: Of or pertaining to a normal.
One fond of his own opinious; one who holds an opinion. [Obs.]Glanvill.
Pertaining to, or resulting from, sexual connection; formed bythe union of the male and female elements.
Jollity; noisy mirth. Chaucer.
Low land overflowed, or covered wholly or partially with water,but producing sedge, coarse grasses, or other aquatic plants; boggyland; moor; marsh.'Mid reedy fens wide spread. Wordsworth.
